messages.body_plain:
geno.table returns allele frequencies; if you use scanone.output=TRUE, the result is in the form produced by scanone, and so you can plot the frequencies just as you'd plot LOD curves. The trick is to find the right columns.

Here's an example:

    library(qtl)
    data(fake.bc)
    gt <- geno.table(fake.bc, scanone.output=TRUE)
    head(gt)
    #         chr   pos neglog10P missing        AA        AB
    #  D1M430   1  0.00 0.0000000  0.7750 0.5000000 0.5000000
    #  D1M318   1  9.80 0.3343524  0.7725 0.5384615 0.4615385
    #  D1M212   1 13.11 0.2800250  0.1100 0.4831461 0.5168539
    #  D1M437   1 37.11 0.5276568  0.5500 0.4611111 0.5388889
    #  D1M490   1 53.51 0.1717978  0.1000 0.4888889 0.5111111
    #  D1M15    1 79.71 0.6863369  0.1000 0.5333333 0.4666667
   plot(gt, lod=3:4, col=c("slateblue", "violetred"),
        bgrect="gray95", bandcol="gray85", ylim=c(0,1))
   plot(gt, lod=2, col="gray70", add=TRUE)

karl

I have some QTL models, where I want to test the significance of a second QTL (and QTL*covariate interaction) in the context of a less complex model.

1: Y ~ Q1 + Q2 + covar
2: Y ~ Q1 + Q2 + Q2*covar + covar
3: Y ~ Q1 + Q2 + Q1*covar + covar
4: Y ~ Q1 + Q1*covar + Q2*covar + covar

So, to get P-values for the Q2 term, I plan to calculate permutations for the 1st and 4th model with the following covariates:
1: scanone(..., addcovar= data.frame(genotypes@Q1, covar), intcovar=NULL)
4: scanone(..., addcovar= data.frame(genotypes@Q1, covar), intcovar=data.frame(covar))

However, it is not clear to me how (or if it is possible) to get permutation tests for the Q2 term in the 2nd and 3rd models.

Any advice is appreciated,
John

messages.subject_clean: [Rqtl-disc] PLOT genotype frequency and genotype missing rate together
messages.body_plain:
I wrote a function a while ago that does this ... may make your life easier. It takes a cross object (class can be "f2", "bc","dh", 'riself") and a vector of your genotype names - if you haven't specified this, you can leave it blank.

For example:
data(multitrait)
plotGT(multitrait)

data(fake.f2)
plotGT(fake.f2)

plotGT<-function(cross, genotype.names=c("AA","AB","BB")){
  gt<-geno.table(cross, scanone.output=TRUE)
  if(class(cross)[1]=="f2"){
    plot(gt, lod=(which(colnames(gt) %in% genotype.names)-2), col=c("blue", "red","green"),
         ylim=c(0,1))
    plot(gt, lod=which(colnames(gt) =="missing")-2, col=c("grey"), add=T)
    legend("topright", c(genotype.names,"NA"), col=c("blue", "red","green", "grey"), lty=1)
    title("segregation distortion and missing data")
  }else{
    plot(gt, lod=(which(colnames(gt) %in% genotype.names)-2), col=c("blue", "red"),
         ylim=c(0,1))
    plot(gt, lod=which(colnames(gt) =="missing")-2, col=c("grey"), add=T)
    legend("topright", c(colnames(gt[5:6]),"NA"), col=c("blue", "red", "grey"), lty=1)
    title("segregation distortion and missing data")
  }
}

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] QTL-specific covariate interactions
messages.body_plain:
My approach is to do permutations just with the covariate (no QTL genotypes in the addcovar data frame).

Let's add model 0: Y ~ Q1 + cover

In comparing 1 to 0, I'd look at

  operm_10 <- scanone(..., addcovar=covar, intcovar=NULL, n.perm=1000)

In comparing 2 to 0, I'd look at

  operm_20 <- scanone(..., addcovar=covar, intcovar=covar, n.perm=1000)

In comparing 3 to 1 (is there a Q1 x covar interaction, I'd look at paired permutations with and without the interaction term:

  set.seed(20150807)
  operm_10 <- scanone(..., addcovar=covar, intcovar=NULL, n.perm=1000)
  set.seed(20150807)
  operm_30 <- scanone(..., addcovar=covar, intcovar=covar, n.perm=1000)
  operm_31 <- operm_30 - operm_10

I'm not sure I understand what's going on with model 4, or what you want to compare it to.

When you talk about tests of significance, it should be for a comparison between two models.

karl

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] QTL-specific covariate interactions
messages.body_plain:
Including the genotypes doesn't quite work, as they end up being made independent of the rest of the genome. My approach has been to use the null hypothesis of no QTL as an approximation of the distribution in the presence of a QTL. With linked QTL, this won't work.

Two alternatives:

 - a parametric bootstrap (simulate data under the fitted single-QTL model)
 - a stratified permutation test (permute the phenotypes within each stratum defined by the genotype at the first QTL)

karl

The LOD scores from scanone compare a model with a single QTL to a model with no QTL.
The LOD scores in your use of fitqtl compare a model with two QTL to a model with one QTL.

So they tend to be different. fitqtl can give LOD scores that are either bigger or smaller; we hope for them to be bigger, but that doesn't always happen.

messages.body_plain:
I'll generally make PDF figures.

In R, you'd use the pdf() function prior to your plotting code, and then dev.off() to close off the file.

  x <- rnorm(100)
  y <- x+rnorm(100, 0.2)

  pdf("myplot.pdf", height=9, width=6.5, pointsize=14)
  plot(x,y)
  dev.off()

There are two basic kinds of image files: bitmaps (such as jpeg, png, and tiff) and vectorized images (such as PDF and SVG). To avoid pixelation, you generally want to use the latter. But for images with *many* elements, the former will provide a much smaller file size.
